_comment: SKILL BLUEPRINT — output of the Spec agent, input to the Generator agent. One blueprint per standard.
subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
description: Students construct two-way frequency tables that classify each object by two categories at once, fill in row totals, column totals, and the grand total, and read the table as a sample space. From the table they compute marginal probabilities (a single category, e.g. $P(\text{senior})$), joint probabilities (the intersection of two categories, e.g. $P(\text{senior and plays a sport})$), and conditional probabilities ($P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$, computed directly from the table as the count in a cell divided by the row or column total). They use these to test whether two events are independent by checking $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$ or, equivalently, $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, and they interpret what dependence means in the data context. Counts come from raw frequencies; probabilities are written as exact fractions or their reduced/decimal equivalents.
subSkills: Construct a two-way frequency table from a verbal description or list, placing each object in the cell matching its two categories
Complete the margins of a table: compute each row total, each column total, and the grand total, and check that row totals and column totals both sum to the grand total
Read a marginal probability from the table as a row or column total over the grand total, e.g. $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{row total}}{\text{grand total}}$
Read a joint probability as a single cell count over the grand total, e.g. $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{\text{cell}}{\text{grand total}}$
Compute a conditional probability $P(B \mid A)$ as the cell count over the conditioning row or column total (the reduced sample space)
Distinguish $P(B \mid A)$ from $P(A \mid B)$ by identifying which total is the denominator
Test independence of two events by checking whether $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$, or equivalently whether $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$
Interpret independence or dependence in context (whether knowing one category changes the likelihood of the other)

problemArchetypes.name: Construct the table and fill margins
problemArchetypes.example: Of $40$ students, $22$ are seniors and the rest juniors; $15$ of the seniors play a sport and $9$ of the juniors play a sport. Build the two-way table of class (senior/junior) versus sport (yes/no) and find all row totals, column totals, and the grand total. Answer: seniors $15$ yes / $7$ no $=22$; juniors $9$ yes / $9$ no $=18$; columns $24$ yes, $16$ no; grand total $40$.

problemArchetypes.name: Marginal probability
problemArchetypes.example: From a table with grand total $40$ and $24$ students who play a sport, find $P(\text{plays a sport})$. Answer: $\dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Joint probability
problemArchetypes.example: From the same table, find $P(\text{senior and plays a sport})$ where that cell holds $15$. Answer: $\dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Conditional probability from a row or column
problemArchetypes.example: Given $15$ of $22$ seniors play a sport, find $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior})$. Answer: $\dfrac{15}{22}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare two conditionals
problemArchetypes.example: Find $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$ and $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{junior}) = \dfrac{9}{18} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and state which group is more likely to play a sport.

problemArchetypes.name: Test independence with the product rule
problemArchetypes.example: With $P(\text{senior}) = \dfrac{22}{40}$, $P(\text{sport}) = \dfrac{24}{40}$, and $P(\text{senior and sport}) = \dfrac{15}{40}$, decide whether class and sport are independent. Check $P(A)\cdot P(B) = \dfrac{22}{40}\cdot\dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{33}{100} = 0.33$ versus $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{15}{40} = 0.375$. They are not equal, so the events are not independent.

problemArchetypes.name: Test independence via conditional equals marginal
problemArchetypes.example: Decide independence by comparing $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22} \approx 0.682$ with $P(\text{sport}) = \dfrac{24}{40} = 0.6$. Since they differ, knowing a student is a senior changes the probability of playing a sport, so the events are dependent.

problemArchetypes.name: Design a table that forces independence
problemArchetypes.example: Fill in the missing cells of a partly completed two-way table so that the two categories are independent, using $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$ to back out each required cell count.

Easy.description: A complete two-way table is given (or a one-cell gap to fill via a margin). The student reads off or completes margins and computes a single marginal or joint probability as a count over the grand total, or fills a missing row/column total. One step, friendly numbers, and probabilities reduce cleanly.
constraints: Table is fully or almost fully provided; at most one missing margin cell to complete by addition
Grand total is small and round (e.g. $20$, $40$, $50$, $100$) so fractions reduce to simple values
Task is a single marginal $\dfrac{\text{row or column total}}{\text{grand total}}$ or joint $\dfrac{\text{cell}}{\text{grand total}}$ probability
No independence test and no conditioning; answer is one reduced fraction or its decimal

Medium.description: The student computes a conditional probability $P(B \mid A)$ using the correct conditioning total, distinguishes it from $P(A \mid B)$, and may build the table from a short verbal description first. Two to three steps: extract counts, identify the right denominator, and reduce.
constraints: Requires conditioning: denominator is a row or column total, not the grand total
May require constructing or completing the table from a verbal description before reading values
Includes at least one comparison of two conditionals (e.g. $P(B \mid A)$ versus $P(B \mid A^c)$) or of a conditional versus a marginal
Numbers may not reduce to unit fractions; exact fraction answers expected

Hard.description: Multi-step independence reasoning over a constructed or partly missing table. The student tests independence by the product rule or by comparing a conditional to a marginal, interprets the result in context, or reverse-engineers cell counts that would make two events independent. Several computations plus a justified conclusion are required.
constraints: Build or complete the table, then formally test independence via $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$ or $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$
Requires a stated conclusion in context (independent vs. dependent and what that means about the data)
May ask the student to fill missing cells so that two events are independent, solving $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$ for an unknown count
Multiple probabilities computed and compared; answers are exact fractions or decimals and a verdict

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: If this standard were built as two worksheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium, constructing and completing two-way tables, computing marginal and joint probabilities from the grand total, and a first pass at conditional probability with the correct conditioning total. tier2 covers Medium to Hard, comparing conditionals, the full independence test by both the product rule and the conditional-equals-marginal rule, contextual interpretation, and back-solving cells that force independence. No item overlap between tiers. The default build is a single 15-item worksheet ramping Easy to Hard.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses the grand total as the denominator for a conditional probability instead of the conditioning row or column total
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{senior})$ with $15$ sport-playing seniors out of $22$ seniors and grand total $40$, reports $\dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$ (the joint probability) instead of $\dfrac{15}{22}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Swaps the condition and the event, computing $P(A \mid B)$ when $P(B \mid A)$ is asked
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Asked for $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays sport})$ but gives $P(\text{plays sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$ instead of $\dfrac{15}{24}$, dividing by the wrong total

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses a joint probability with a conditional probability
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Asked for $P(\text{senior and sport})$ gives the conditional $\dfrac{15}{22}$ instead of $\dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tests independence by checking whether events are mutually exclusive rather than whether $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes class and sport are independent only because the 'senior and sport' cell is nonzero, or calls them independent because some students are both, instead of comparing $P(A \cap B)$ with $P(A)\cdot P(B)$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adds the marginal probabilities instead of multiplying them when applying the independence product rule
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Tests independence with $P(A) + P(B) = \dfrac{22}{40} + \dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{46}{40}$ instead of $P(A)\cdot P(B) = \dfrac{22}{40}\cdot\dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{33}{100}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Mis-completes the table by summing across the wrong dimension, mixing up row and column totals
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports a row total by adding down a column (or vice versa), so the margins no longer sum to the grand total, e.g. listing the senior total as $24$ (a column count) instead of $22$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to reduce or leaves the probability as a raw count rather than a fraction over a total
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives the answer as $15$ (the cell count) or $\dfrac{15}{1}$ instead of the probability $\dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Declares dependence whenever the conditional and marginal are merely close, without checking exact equality, or declares independence when they differ slightly
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Sees $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22} \approx 0.68$ and $P(\text{sport}) = 0.6$ and calls them independent ('about the same') instead of recognizing $0.68 \ne 0.6$ means dependent

_comment_itemCounts: worksheet.single = one ramped sheet (Easy->Hard across 15 items). tier1/tier2 only if the standard is split into two worksheets (15 each, no overlap).
